topics.title: Not_Richard's Super Secret Squaring Technique
topics.text:
We all know Richard Ruczyk has a Super Secret Squaring Technique, but what about Not_Richard? Well it turns out he has one too for numbers {40, 50}! I met him in the halls the other day and asked him to square 43. This is what he did:

43-25=18

50-43=7   =>   7^2=49.

18 & 49   =>   1849.



I didn't believe him, so I checked it on my calculator later that day, and it worked!

The next day I asked him to square 48, confident he would fail:

48-25=23

50-48=2   =>   2^2=04 (note how he turns '4' into a two digit number '04')

23 & 04   =>   2304



It worked again!

At this point, Genius_4_Life came along and told us that a modification of his technique would work for ANY number>25.

This is what the method was:

Step 1: Take the number x and evaluate x-25. Then add two zero's to the end where step two will go. This is A.

Step 2: Subtract x from 50. Then square that value. This is B.

Step 3: A+B is le square. The reason for two zeros in Step 1 is so that for 3-digit and higher values of B.



Prove that this works.

topics.text:
Johny has $3J$ dollars. He has the following bank offers that he will use:



Nacho Bank: We triple the money you put in, and halve that.  So, $\frac{3J}{2}$

Hamburger Bank: We double the money you put that and split that into thirds. You get $\frac{1}{3}$. So $\frac{2J}{3}$.

Bank Bank: Every day you get $\frac{J}{100}$ dollars per day.



Problem sheet:



A1) If Johny puts $J$ into each bank, over $46$ days how much money will he have in terms of $J$?

A2) What if $J=26$?

topics.title: k Dear MATHCOUNTS, An Open Letter (My 500th Post on AoPS)
topics.text:
Dear MATHCOUNTS,



I hope this is an adequate way of saying thank you for what you have given me through your competition series over the last three years. What I have done in your competitions has changed me forever, and I am certain I will never forget those moments. MATHCOUNTS has changed me in so many ways, and I would like to say here what happened to me during my MATHCOUNTS career so you know what difference you can make in someone.



Few people (I hope) remember how I was around age 10: shy, childish, you name it. I had absolutely no self-confidence. The previous year or two I had started to do math at home and I had gotten pretty good, but my contest scores still weren't great and I felt I was a failure at everything. I wasn't that good at any sport either, so I felt there was no use for my super-competitive juices, which remain today a really strong part of my personality. Of course, this is when I discover MATHCOUNTS.



My story starts in fifth grade, the year before I start MATHCOUNTS. Based on various other milestones one could argue that my story starts somewhere else, but inside I feel my story starts in fifth grade. My memories of school were very fond, I had a great teacher and many good friends. But it was also when I started math competitions. I had already been doing serious training in MATHCOUNTS and the AMC 8. We tried to convince my school to let me do the AMC 8 in school, but after long deliberation they decided they didn't want any lower schoolers doing the AMC 8. So I went to a math club nearby which I was not a member of to take it. They were very nice to let me in, as I believe I was the only non-member there, and definitely the youngest. The test was late at night, and before I went into the competition room I ate some candy to keep myself awake. The adrenaline rush that I got before the test was something I would feel countless times in the future as I got ready for other competitions. I thought I did okay on that test going out, and later I learned I got an 18, and got onto the Honor Roll. That was a big achievement for me in my first contest ever. My dad decided to take me to my local Chapter Competition's Countdown Round. Of course, I didn't participate, but it was really inspirational watching the kids solve them quickly. I even saw some people I knew. But now I'm sure I know everybody who was in the room that day. They would give questions to the audience, and I remember getting the question: "What is the larger number of the two prime numbers that sum to 12,345?" right, and I was the only person to raise my hand. This was the beginning of what would be an incredible MATHCOUNTS career.



Moving on to sixth grade, when I started middle school. We started a MATHCOUNTS club in my school, because we had never had one before and I really wanted to do MATHCOUNTS. We got incredible participation that first year. 29 people came to the School Competition. Even after all that training, that test I felt so nervous, partly because it was my first competitive MATHCOUNTS ever. I won that competition and got onto the team, and was counting down the days until the Chapter Competition. At this point people would routinely come to me to ask for math homework help, and this was the first real respect I ever had I think. In previous years I was just the shy kid who's pretty good at math. I still remember that night before the Chapter Competition in sixth grade, I couldn't sleep. I was simply waiting for the super-exciting competition to come. These are the moments you live for I think. I met up with my team early Saturday morning at school, and we carpooled to the competition. It was as amazing as I thought it would be. There was a sign we saw that said "MATHCOUNTS Registration" and I start getting this amazing feeling inside, that I'd actually be a part of this forever. After waiting for a while, they sat us down in a large auditorium to take the test. When I took the test, I was actually sick that day so I had tissues next to me, but I didn't use them because I was so excited. I went through the test at a relatively good speed, getting to around #27 on the Sprint Round. The Target Round was as expected, I easily got the easy ones but didn't really do well on the harder ones. We were then moved to another room for the Team Round, and we were confident on the first 9, but then my team and I were clueless on #10 so I guessed. It turned out to be right! When we went to eat lunch, I had never felt so nervous. I knew I had a legitimate shot at Countdown, and I really wanted to make it as a sixth-grader. I barely ate any lunch, and finally they came out and announced who made Countdown. And for some reason, my name was last on the list. Name by name they called and it wasn't mine, and I got super nervous, and then finally my name, but no! A different last name! But then they call my full name, and I go up super relieved that not only did I make Countdown but I made States too. In the first round, my first question was: "How many terminal zeros are at the end of 125!?" I buzzed in immediately with the correct answer of 31. Even the moderator had to look for a second at me before telling me it was correct. No one in that entire room had gotten it right that fast. The second question had something to do with regular polygons, which I also got. I looked at the crowd and smiled. I knew I had a future at this. The next round I was beaten on the first question, and my opponent had a large cheering group, so I felt really nervous. But then I rattled off three correct answers out of the next four (the other one neither of us got), so I was in the finals. And I was playing a kid who was a good friend of mine, and we always were neck-and-neck everywhere. The questions got harder and kudos to him, he was faster than me. He won 3-0, so I got second. My team also got fourth. I got fifth individually. The feeling after that competition, however, was like something I had never felt before. I eagerly awaited the State Competition. When it finally came, I remember the wait was even longer. We went into a small classroom this time, just me and my three teammates with some of the other teams, with a proctor or two. I was also sick that day and I was coughing a lot. The test was really hard this time, and I knew from the beginning that I wasn't making Nationals. I might not have even made Countdown. After skipping almost half of the questions, I went back to check my work. I fixed a few answers, then time was called. I was really unhappy. The Target and Team rounds went by quickly, and I remember doing okay on the two of them. Then we ate pizza for lunch and I played on my phone. I was once again really nervous for Countdown. This would, obviously, become a common feeling for me. When they finally announced the Countdown names, my name was first this time (phew!) and I went up and sat in one of the seats next to the stage. My first round I was super nervous and buzzed in early every time, almost every time with the wrong answer. Except I got one right, and that was enough to put me into the next round. In the next round I had never felt more pressure: a win and I am guaranteed a trophy at States in sixth grade. What an incredible achievement that would be! Again I was super nervous, and I buzzed in early, only once with the correct answer, but that was enough. (I later learned that kid got 1st at Written!) In the Semifinals I got destroyed by the eventual champion, I didn't even stand a chance. The third place match was more interesting, though. I was playing another sixth-grader (this year, we were teammates at Nationals.) I got the first two questions really quickly, but then the next two I got nervous and got them wrong, and he took his time and got them right. The next correct answer would win third place, and I went a tiny bit slower, and still got the next question faster. I won third place in Countdown! But then when they said the top teams and individuals (I got 11th I later learned, and my team got 10th), it hit me that I didn't make Nationals. It hit me really hard. That feeling would stay with me until the State Competition the next year.



Now I was in seventh grade, and I had more self-confidence than a lot of kids at my school. The experience I had at MATHCOUNTS the previous year stayed with me, and I was always smiling, as if I was always remembering that moment. I was sick again (can you believe my luck?) for the School Competition that year, so sick I shouldn't have gone to school. But I knew if I didn't go to school I would have no chance at Nationals, so I went. I got a 44 on the competition, and first at my school. That gave me confidence for future competitions that year. I didn't really train prior to the Chapter Competition, knowing that I had already gotten 5th in sixth grade and that I was a substantial favorite to get a trophy this time. It was the biggest mistake of my MATHCOUNTS career. Again I was super excited for the competition, that whole week it was the only thing I thought about. I really wanted that feeling of being in the competition room again. When we met at school again, my mind was racing. All I was thinking about was lunch and Countdown, and I wasn't paying any heed to the Written component. When we showed up we were in a different building this time, which kind of bummed me out because I didn't feel as comfortable as I did the previous year, having been in the same place as watching it in fifth grade. They took us upstairs for the written component, and I raced through the Sprint Round, seeing how easy the questions looked after another year of MATHCOUNTS training. The Target Round also went quickly, with only one very hard question (and evidently one other silly after I saw my score.) Our team was much better this year even though we lost a lot of 8th-graders, because everyone had an extra year of training. We did very well on the Team Round, and I went down feeling very confident about myself. However, I still felt that feeling of absolute nervousness, something I had only felt two times before in my life: pre-Countdown at the Chapter and State rounds the year before. Yet again my name was first, so there was no time to be nervous. I was relieved I made Countdown, feeling like there was a lot of pressure on me. But in the first round of Countdown I was playing a kid who I recognized from the previous year, and he improved a lot. He beat me on the first question, but I beat him on the second question, and the tension was unbearable. I made a silly mistake on the next question, and that was it, he got it right and the dream was over. I sulked through the rest of the Countdown Round, and then it didn't help that I wasn't one of the top individuals (I later learned I got 6th individually, worse than last year). My team got 2nd, which was the one exciting part on the day. We were really building as a team and we had a great future. I just hoped I would one-up myself at States, and I really wanted to make Nationals as a seventh-grader. The year before it had been so painful when I didn't qualify for Nationals, and I didn't want that to happen again. I doubled my daily math training from one hour to two hours that month, and did only MATHCOUNTS-specific training, meaning I halted my AoPS studies. I couldn't sleep again before the State Competition, this time knowing I had something to play for. I wanted to make Nationals so badly. We had a practice at my house the night before and met at my house early in the morning again. But it snowed, and the competition was delayed by a couple of hours!!!! And even worse, they cancelled the Countdown Round!!!! It was really really tense at the competition, and we waited for a while before they finally gave us the test. I saw some kids I knew very well, and I went through the Sprint Round and managed to finish it. Speed was something I payed lots of attention to the month before Chapters, because I knew I needed as many correct answers as possible if I wanted a chance at making Nationals. After a pretty good Sprint Round, the Target Round was okay and I answered most of them. The Team Round was okay, but it was much harder than last year, unlike the rest of the test. I thought they were playing with teams that used the evens and odds trick on the Team Round, and it was really hard. Lunchtime that day was even more nerve-racking because there was no Countdown Round. There was a long lecture about prime numbers that wasn’t great, and I was really nervous. They finally announced the top four teams first. Our school was third! It made me more confident about my chances at making Nationals. The fourth-place individual wasn't me, but the third-place individual was! As I walked to get my trophy, I felt like I was walking at Nationals. I was so excited about what was going to happen. I continued to train for another couple of months, and I was really nervous because I wanted to make the Countdown Round. I had always watched other people in the National Countdown Round, and that was my dream above all dreams. However, as a seventh-grader it seemed unlikely for me to actually do it. The practices and train ride with my teammates were really fun, but in the end it was time to meet some AoPSers. I got a lot of pins at the National Competition being a very serious pin-trader (every state has a different kind of pin and you try to trade with other states), and the hotel was fun but then when I went into the competition room it was all business. I wanted to do as well as I possibly could. After all the chants, we started. I was really nervous the whole time and quickly got under time pressure. I didn't make it to the end of the competition, and it was really heartbreaking. I knew for the first time in my MATHCOUNTS career I would have to watch the Countdown Round as a spectator. The Target Round whizzed by and I did okay on it, as did the Team Round which we practiced so hard for. Then they ushered us into this giant room and gave us all clappers. I saw people leaving the room, teams leaving the room. When we got close to the front I realized what was happening. I saw Arkansas run in, and I heard the announcer calling the states. So it was actually true! I got to run in to the light show at Nationals! Although I didn't make Countdown or win any award (congrats Kevin Liu), it was still a dream come true. I learned later that I got 143rd individually and my team got 26th, and I hoped to only improve this year.



By eighth grade (this year) I was no longer a shy kid at school. The National Competition made me proud of who I was, made me proud of being a member of the elite group that got to go to Nationals. And I would have the opportunity to do it twice! When the School Competition came around, I had barely touched a MATHCOUNTS test, save for a couple of practice Nationals. I tried the same strategy that worked for me last year, going really fast. Unfortunately this year I was a lot more silly mistake prone, and I made many many silly mistakes, and I got 3rd in my school. This just made me want to study harder, to get redemption, because I knew I was better than that. I knew that I had a shot at doing great things at Nationals as an 8th-grader, and I knew that I would need a stronger performance at Chapters. In the calendar year 2016 I didn't learn any new math during the MATHCOUNTS season, only MATHCOUNTS problems. I did a combination of using AoPS's MATHCOUNTS Trainer and the MATHCOUNTS OPLET on the MATHCOUNTS site. I immediately saw my scores on practice tests skyrocket. For the first time, not only was I avoiding silly mistakes, but I was also getting 40s and above on practice Chapter, State, and even old National competitions. This made the anticipation prior to the Chapter Competition even more unbearable. Our team was better than it ever was before, and we made a goal at the start of the year to win the state championship. My coach went with me to the National Competition a year before because the first and second place coaches couldn't go, but this year we wanted to win it outright. The Chapter Competition as always came with a lot of anticipation and lots of practice tests. But on the day of the test I felt surprisingly calm. I had been in the situation two, or maybe even three (if you count watching in 5th grade) times before, and I was simply a different person now. This was another way MATHCOUNTS has changed me, I have learned how to handle immense pressure. We went to the same room as last time, and I went through the test way more cautious than I did at the School Competition. I knew that a handful of silly mistakes would keep me from Countdown, and I definitely didn't want that to happen. However, I went so slow that I only made it to #27, even though I finished it last year! The Target Round was a different story, besides a silly mistake on #2 I went through the rest smoothly. Our amazing team crushed the Team Round, and I felt pretty good come lunchtime. However, the nerves came in again. It was my last Chapter Countdown ever should I qualify, and I really didn't want the heartbreak of sixth grade or the disgrace of seventh grade in the Countdown Round. I really felt this year was my year. But I was still nervous. They called my name in the middle of the pack, and I went up only to face something I had never faced before in MATHCOUNTS: I was playing a school teammate in the first round of the Countdown Round. Not just a school teammate, but one of my best friends since I started going to this certain school. It was painful every time I got a question right because I knew that one of my teammates was losing, but I did win the match. The semifinals I played against the kid who won the Chapter Competition last year, and it was nail-biting but I managed to win that one too. But then in the final I played against someone else from my school. When we do practice Countdowns at school it would very often end up as me against him, and now we were playing for the Chapter Competition finals. It reached 2-2, but then neither of us could get a question right. It was like writer's block, but for math. Neither one of us could finish the other one off. Finally, after the good part of 10 questions, I got one right and I won the Countdown Round. It was jubilation, but I also felt bad because I had to beat two teammates in the process. At the awards ceremony, I learned I got 2nd individually and our team got 1st. This gave me huge confidence going into the State Competition. But with huge confidence came even harder work, and sometimes I was working two and a half to three hours a day to finish what I was doing. I wanted to make Nationals so hard, I didn't want it to be even in doubt this time. I wanted to be able to make it on the worst of days, so I wouldn't feel nervous. But even with all the studying and all the practice tests, the day before I had that same feeling in my stomach which I would learn to love and now miss. The pre-competition feeling. The next day we met at school and got into carpooling groups, and we went to the competition. As always, there was tons of waiting time, and we were standing around for a while. But when the dust cleared and we got into the same small classroom, I felt that same feeling again. That same room I had been in for the previous two years was the room we were in again, and I knew it would be the last time. I closed my eyes, took a deep breath and then started the Sprint Round. I started slow, but then sped up as I felt more comfortable with my speed. However, I still didn't make it to the end of the test; all the work to reduce silly mistakes meant that I went much much slower. In fact, I only answered 23 on the State Competition, compared to the 26 or 27 from the previous year. But I still felt confident as I breezed through the Target Round (except for the last question), which meant that it would be down to how many silly mistakes I made to see whether I made the National Competition. Before the Countdown Round I met a new definition of nervous. I felt like the pressure was on me, and that I had to do at States what I did at Chapters. When they announced the Countdown people, my name was towards the end. We were all really nervous that I didn't even make Countdown, let alone Nationals. But I did, and then in my first round match I won on a deciding question that I would've lost if it weren't for my opponent buzzing in first incorrectly (I had the same answer as him.) In the second round, however, I didn't have the same luck. My opponent won the deciding question off of what he later told me was a guess. Oh well, I thought, there goes my Countdown career. (It would be my last competitive Countdown match ever.) I didn't pay much attention to the rest of the Countdown Round, waiting restlessly for the awards ceremony. Countdown came first, and obviously I got nothing. Then they said teams, and we got first! We hit our goal for the year, and we were state champions! Then the top individuals were announced. I wasn't 4th or 3rd. I thought to myself, "I don't care if you make me 1st or 2nd. Just say my name." Sure enough, I was 2nd! Although it didn't come with the added bonus of winning the state championship, I made Nationals! It was a really exciting moment for me, and I wanted to study really hard for Nationals so I could be my best. However, looking retrospectively on the ensuing two months, I can say I had too much of a life. I had other things going on, including school and tennis tournaments, to be able to study lights out for Nationals. Albeit I studied more than was humanly possible given my restrictions, but looking back it simply wasn't enough. I went to my team practices, and met my new teammates who were all really nice, and when our train arrived in Washington, DC I was so excited for what was going to come next. Unfortunately, I was sick again. The first day was bad because I was using a tissue every day. And because I missed the AoPS party the previous year, I made an extra effort to meet a lot of AoPSers this time. I went to both AoPS parties and I had a lot of fun there. I traded lots of pins and got every one except for the Virgin Islands. But on the competition, after the cheers, when the flashcards went back in my backpack and my calculator went to the proctor for the Sprint Round, there was adrenaline of course but something just wasn't clicking. It wasn't exhaustion, although I barely slept the night before, but there was something else hindering me. I made it through the first 10, after skipping some questions, in 15 minutes. It was never the same after that. I did better, but I made it to #23, which was an improvement given I made it that far at States two months earlier. But still I had no more chances at Countdown. Although I did well on the first 4 Target Round questiond and got some Countdown hope, I basically fell asleep on #s 5 and 6. Those two problems were a nightmare come true. I was daydreaming of myself in the Countdown Round, and then I heard time called as soon as I started working on the problems. Instantly the daydream went away, never to return. I did alright on #s 7 and 8, then basically zoned out on the Team Round. I knew my MATHCOUNTS career was over and I was so sad. The run-in was absolutely amazing again, and even though I wasn't in the Countdown Round everybody was amazing. It's incredible to think someone actually got a perfect on this test! Congratulations Edward Wan! But then I truly realized my MATHCOUNTS career was over, and it was definitely one of the most bittersweet moments of my life. I was so sad that it was over, yet so happy that I got the opportunity to go to Nationals twice in three tries. I later learned that I got 71st individually and the highest in my state, one question away from Top 56. My team got 25th.



To conclude, I would like to state one more time how grateful I am for the MATHCOUNTS competitions. MATHCOUNTS, if you ever read this, just know that you changed my life forever. As I sit here writing this post, I probably should be studying for 8th-grade exams. I'm evidently almost done with middle school, and I'm taking the time to reflect on what has really been an incredible journey for me. Once again, thank you so much for what you have done.



Sincerely,

topics.title: Money exchanges in a game called Animal Jam
topics.text:
Animal Jam is a fun game that's actually made by National Geographic. In Animal Jam, there are three money units: gems, diamonds, and tickets. You can exchange diamonds for gems in this game. Time for the math. The exchanges you can make are:



1 diamond - 1,000 gems

4 diamonds - 5,000 gems

7 diamonds - 10,000 gems

10 diamonds - 15,000 gems



Let's figure out the maximum number of gems you can get with a fixed number of diamonds. Looks pretty tricky. I thought linear programming was the key to solving this, but it wasn't.

I was talking about this stuff with my father last night. The good thing about this is 1, 4, 7, and 10 are in an arithmetic sequence. This leads to some ideas... Let's say you had 8 diamonds. Should you do the first and third exchanges, or two of the second exchange? You will get more gems doing the first and third exchange. Hey, this means you should never do two of the second exchange, because you'll get more gems doing the first and third! What if we had 11 diamonds? Should we do the first and fourth exchange, or the second and third? Do the first and fourth exchange, you will get more gems. This means don't do both the second and third exchanges to maximize your gems, you'll get more doing the first and fourth. And what about if you had 14 diamonds? Do you do the second and fourth exchange, or the third exchange twice? It actually doesn't matter. You'll get the same number of gems either way. Another thing: We have 21 diamonds this time. Should we do three of the third exchange, or two of the fourth and the first exchange once? We do the fourth exchange twice and the first once to get more gems. We see from this that you do not do the third exchange three times, because you get even more gems doing the fourth exchange twice and the fourth exchange once. And don't do the first exchange 4 or more times because you can replace that with doing the second exchange! Lastly, we look at the quality of each exchange (gems/diamonds). They have qualities of 1,000, 1,250, 1,429, and 1,500, respectively. It seems like we should just do as many of the fourth exchange as possible, and keep doing the biggest exchange possible. This is the answer (I think)! In fact, we could of just guessed this from the very beginning (ooh, maybe I didn't have to go through all that annoying stuff to get the answer)! But if we have different numbers, it gets harder.



There's also gems to tickets exchanges in Animal Jam. But it's not very interesting, because for all the exchanges, you pay a number of gems, and get exactly twice as many tickets. You can basically do what you want. The end.
